analysis.one_liner: Requires the biggest banks to hold a reserve equal to the government bailout subsidy they receive.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have required the largest banks to reserve the value of their government bailout guarantee, never advanced beyond a committee referral and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Large financial firms benefit when markets expect the government to rescue them if they fail — that expectation lowers their borrowing costs. The bill would have directed the Federal Reserve to calculate the dollar value of that implicit bailout guarantee for each of the biggest firms and required them to hold that amount in a reserve they could not count toward regulatory capital. The reserve could only shrink if the firm sold assets or spun off subsidiaries, effectively penalizing size and complexity. It died in committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers and bank customers would benefit from an additional cushion at the largest firms, funded by the value of the implicit bailout guarantee, reducing the chance that a bank failure lands on the public. Smaller banks that do not enjoy the same implicit subsidy would also compete on slightly more even footing.

how_it_helps.text: It would require the biggest bank holding companies and supervised nonbank financial companies to set aside an amount each year equal to the value of the implicit government backstop, so taxpayers are not the ones implicitly financing too-big-to-fail.
The reserve could only shrink if the company divests assets, giving large firms an incentive to shrink rather than rely on the subsidy.

analysis.who_pays: The largest bank holding companies and systemically important nonbank firms, which would have to set aside the estimated value of their implicit government guarantee and could not count it toward capital requirements, locking up funds that would otherwise support lending, dividends, or buybacks.

drawbacks.text: Because the reserve cannot count toward capital requirements, banks would effectively have to hold extra funds beyond existing rules, a cost that could be passed to customers or that critics would say reduces lending capacity.

The Fed would have to devise a formula to measure an implicit subsidy — an expectation about future government behavior — which is inherently uncertain and would likely be contested heavily in rulemaking.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit would be that the largest financial firms hold a cushion sized to the government backstop they enjoy, potentially sparing the public from funding future bailouts; the cost is that capital locked in a reserve cannot be redeployed, which critics would argue reduces lending, and the reserve stacks on top of existing capital rules rather than replacing anything, making its real-world effect hard to predict. As drafted, it never advanced far enough for the tradeoffs to be tested in committee.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in June 2013 and referred to the House Financial Services Committee, where it sat with no cosponsors and no action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The House introduced the bill on June 5, 2013 and referred it the same day to the Committee on Financial Services.
The bill never gained a single cosponsor.
No committee markup, hearing, or floor vote is recorded in the action history; the bill died at the end of the 113th Congress in January 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The largest banks are better off, since they keep the implicit government bailout subsidy without being required to reserve for it. Taxpayers remain exposed to the cost of future failures of systemically important firms.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The largest banks, which keep the implicit subsidy

for.name: Rep. Michael Capuano
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 5, 2013 and it was referred to committee.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.what_they_did: Never took the bill up after referral; no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the record.

against.name: House leadership
against.what_they_did: Allowed the bill to die in committee with no floor consideration; well-known that a bill without committee action cannot reach the floor.

sides.party_line_note: With no votes taken and zero cosponsors from either party, no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.industry: Largest bank holding companies and systemically important nonbank financial firms
industries.note: These firms would have to lock up the estimated value of their implicit government guarantee in a reserve, reducing funds available for other purposes, and could only release it by shrinking. The implicit subsidy is a real competitive advantage over smaller banks.
